rationale: B wins because it is stricter about what the facts can actually support and gives the founder more usable routes: data, distribution, pricing, and a named-customer feature. Its best move is keeping "Mindbody bundles its AI assistant into existing plans, skipping the AI surcharge" as a distinct business-model angle while warning that the private-company link needs confirmation. A is strong, but "Mindbody owns both the studio's booking system and ClassPass — now its AI sits on top of both" overstates the supplied facts, then tries to walk itself back in the proof section. That is the kind of clever angle that can get a founder into trouble if it leaves the room unqualified.
gaps_in_A: "now its AI sits on top of both" is too confident. The update says Mindbody owns ClassPass, not that the assistant uses or affects ClassPass inventory.
"using aggregated booking data across the network" is an inference, not a supplied fact. The update only says booking data; the proof section should not rescue an overclaimed setup.
The ClassPass angle belongs closer to the uncomfortable-questions section unless Mindbody can prove product interaction, data flow, or marketplace effect.
gaps_in_B: "most boutique studios will never buy an AI tool" is invented market color. Plausible is not the same as sourced.
"a private owner doesn't have to show public markets an AI revenue line" is a smart inference, but it risks laundering the take-private fact into a pricing thesis the update did not supply.
The trend angle's "yield-management thinking arriving at Main Street wellness businesses" is a little consultant-smooth; it needs a studio economics proof point before pitching.
